title: Principles of Marketing
description: A tour of how organizations create, communicate, and deliver value to customers profitably. You will study consumer behavior, segmentation and positioning, and the full marketing mix — product, price, place, and promotion — including digital and social channels, with worked numeric examples throughout.
outcomes: You can explain the marketing concept and analyze a company's environment with a SWOT analysis.
You can segment a market, choose a target, and write a positioning statement.
You can place a product on the product life cycle and recommend a stage-appropriate strategy.
You can calculate cost-plus price, markup percentage, and break-even volume for a pricing decision.
You can compare distribution channel structures and choose one that fits a product's needs.
You can design an integrated marketing communications plan that mixes advertising, PR, and digital channels.

units.title: Foundations of Marketing
units.summary: Marketing is not advertising bolted onto a finished product — it's the discipline of building the whole business around customer value, guided by the environment the firm competes in.

lessons.title: What Marketing Is and Creating Customer Value
lessons.intro: Marketing gets blamed for junk mail and pop-up ads, but its real job is figuring out what customers actually value and making sure the company delivers it better than competitors do.

sections.heading: The Marketing Concept
body: The **marketing concept** holds that a firm succeeds by identifying customer needs and delivering value better than competitors, rather than starting with what's easy to make and pushing it onto buyers. This flips the old **production concept** (assume customers just want cheap, available products) and the **selling concept** (assume customers must be persuaded to buy what the company already makes).

A firm practicing the marketing concept designs products around research into what customers actually want, prices to match perceived value, and treats advertising as communicating real benefits rather than manufacturing demand for a product nobody asked for.

sections.heading: Customer Value and the Exchange
body: **Customer value** is the ratio of perceived benefits to price paid; customers choose the offer that maximizes this ratio among their options, not simply the cheapest one. A $6 coffee can deliver more value than a $1 coffee if the benefits (quality, ambiance, convenience) outweigh the price gap for that customer.

Marketing exists because of **exchange** — both parties give up something to get something they value more. For an exchange to happen, both parties must communicate, and each must believe the value is worth the price, which is why understanding perceived value, not just cost, drives marketing decisions.

example.problem: A regional coffee chain sells drip coffee for $2.50 while a competitor charges $1.25 for a similar cup. Yet the $2.50 chain has more loyal repeat customers. Explain this using customer value.
steps: Customer value is the ratio of perceived benefits to price, not price alone.
If the $2.50 chain's ambiance, consistency, and loyalty rewards raise perceived benefits enough, its value ratio can exceed the cheaper competitor's for its target customers.
example.answer: The $2.50 chain wins loyalty because its added perceived benefits outweigh the price gap for its target customers, giving it a higher value ratio despite the higher price.

keyTerms.def: The philosophy that a firm succeeds by identifying and delivering customer value better than competitors.
The ratio of perceived benefits to price paid, which customers use to compare offers.
A transaction where both parties give up something to get something they value more.

practice.q: The marketing concept differs from the selling concept because it:
choices: Starts with customer needs rather than pushing an already-made product
practice.explain: The marketing concept begins with identified customer needs; the selling concept starts with an existing product and tries to persuade buyers.

practice.q: Customer value is best defined as:
choices: The ratio of perceived benefits to price
The lowest price available in the market
The number of features a product has
practice.explain: Customers compare offers by perceived benefits relative to price, not price or features alone.

practice.q: For an exchange to occur, both parties must:
choices: Believe the value received is worth what they give up
practice.explain: Exchange requires each party to see the trade as worth more than what they gave up.

lessons.title: The Marketing Environment and SWOT Analysis
lessons.intro: No marketing plan survives contact with the real world unless it accounts for competitors, economic shifts, and forces the company can't control. SWOT analysis is the standard tool for taking stock before you plan.

sections.heading: Microenvironment and Macroenvironment
body: The **microenvironment** includes forces close to the firm that it can partly influence: customers, competitors, suppliers, and distribution partners. The **macroenvironment** includes broader forces the firm cannot control: economic conditions, technology, demographics, culture, and law and regulation.

A rising interest rate (macroenvironment) might shrink customers' discretionary spending regardless of how good a firm's product is, while a new competitor's price cut (microenvironment) is something the firm can respond to directly through its own pricing or positioning.

sections.heading: SWOT Analysis
body: **SWOT analysis** organizes planning around Strengths and Weaknesses (internal, controllable) and Opportunities and Threats (external, from the environment). Strengths and weaknesses come from inside the firm — brand reputation, cost structure, talent; opportunities and threats come from scanning the microenvironment and macroenvironment.

A good SWOT is specific and comparative, not generic: 'strong brand loyalty in the 18-24 segment' is useful, while 'good reputation' is not, because it gives no direction for strategy. The output should feed directly into a strategy that uses strengths to capture opportunities and shores up weaknesses against threats.

example.problem: A local bakery is planning next year's strategy. Strength: loyal neighborhood following. Weakness: no online ordering. Opportunity: a nearby office park is adding 2,000 workers. Threat: a national chain is opening two blocks away.
steps: Match the strength to the opportunity: use the loyal following to build word-of-mouth catering business with the incoming office workers.
Address the weakness that blocks capturing that opportunity: build online ordering before the office park opens, since office workers expect to order ahead.
example.answer: Launch online ordering aimed at the office park's lunch crowd, converting existing local loyalty into a new revenue stream before the national chain can capture it.

keyTerms.def: Forces close to the firm — customers, competitors, suppliers — that it can partly influence.
Broad, uncontrollable forces such as the economy, technology, demographics, and law.
A planning framework organizing internal Strengths/Weaknesses against external Opportunities/Threats.

practice.q: A new interest rate hike affecting customer spending is part of the:
practice.explain: Interest rates are a broad, uncontrollable economic force, placing them in the macroenvironment.

practice.q: In SWOT analysis, 'weaknesses' refer to:
choices: Internal, controllable shortcomings of the firm
practice.explain: Weaknesses are internal and controllable, unlike threats, which come from the external environment.

practice.q: A useful SWOT entry should be:
choices: Specific and comparative, giving clear strategic direction
practice.explain: Specific entries like a named customer segment give direction; vague entries like 'good reputation' don't.

lessons.title: Marketing Strategy and the Marketing Plan
lessons.intro: A great product idea without a plan for who to sell it to and how is just a hobby. Marketing strategy turns environmental analysis into a concrete, budgeted plan of action.

sections.heading: From Mission to Marketing Objectives
body: Marketing strategy cascades from the firm's mission (its broad purpose) to overall corporate objectives, then to specific, measurable **marketing objectives** such as 'increase market share in the Southeast region from 8% to 12% within 18 months.' Vague aims like 'grow the brand' can't be executed against or measured.

Objectives should follow SMART criteria — specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time-bound — the same discipline used in goal-setting research across management. A marketing plan without measurable objectives has no way to tell success from failure at the end of the period.

sections.heading: The Marketing Mix as the Plan's Core
body: Once objectives are set, the plan specifies the **marketing mix** — the four Ps of Product, Price, Place, and Promotion — as the levers used to reach the target market and hit the objective. Each P must be internally consistent: a premium product priced high needs premium placement and promotion messaging, not a discount-store presence.

The plan also sets a budget and a timeline, and defines how results will be measured against the original objectives (sales, market share, brand awareness surveys). Without this feedback loop, a firm repeats the same plan next year regardless of whether it actually worked.

example.problem: A new energy-drink brand sets the objective: 'capture 5% of the regional energy-drink market within one year.' Draft a consistent marketing mix.
steps: Product: position as a bold, high-caffeine drink targeting young athletes, distinct from mainstream brands.
Price: match competitor pricing to avoid signaling a cheap knockoff.
Place: secure shelf space in gyms, convenience stores near campuses, and sporting-goods retailers where the target customer already shops.
Promotion: sponsor local college sports teams and run social media campaigns featuring student athletes, consistent with the bold, youth-focused positioning.
example.answer: A consistent mix — competitively priced, distributed through gyms and campus-adjacent stores, promoted via athlete sponsorships and social media — supports the 5% share objective by reaching young athletes where they shop and consume media.

keyTerms.def: A specific, measurable target for a marketing effort, such as a market share or sales goal.
Product, Price, Place, and Promotion — the controllable levers a marketing plan combines.
A goal that is specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time-bound.

practice.q: Which of these is a properly SMART marketing objective?
choices: Increase Southeast market share from 8% to 12% within 18 months
Be the best in the industry
practice.explain: It is specific, measurable, and time-bound, unlike the vague alternatives.

practice.q: The four Ps of the marketing mix are:
practice.explain: The classic marketing mix is Product, Price, Place, and Promotion.

practice.q: A premium-positioned product should generally be paired with:
choices: Premium placement and messaging consistent with a high price
The lowest possible price to gain share fast
practice.explain: Internal consistency across the marketing mix means a premium price needs matching premium placement and promotion, not discount positioning.

units.title: Understanding and Choosing Customers
units.summary: Before you can sell to everyone, figure out who's actually worth selling to. Learn how buyers decide, how to split a market into meaningful groups, and how to claim a distinct position in their minds.

lessons.title: Consumer Buying Behavior
lessons.intro: Buying a pack of gum and buying a car involve wildly different mental processes, and knowing which process a purchase triggers tells you how to market it.

sections.heading: The Buyer Decision Process
body: Consumers typically move through five stages: need recognition, information search, evaluation of alternatives, purchase decision, and post-purchase evaluation. Marketing can intervene at each stage — advertising can trigger need recognition, reviews and content support information search, and a good return policy improves post-purchase evaluation.

**Post-purchase cognitive dissonance** — doubt about whether the purchase was right, especially for expensive items — is common after high-involvement purchases and is why car dealers send confirming follow-up emails and warranties reassure buyers after the sale.

sections.heading: Involvement and Influences on Buying
body: **High-involvement purchases** (a car, a house, a college) involve extensive search and careful evaluation because the cost of a wrong choice is high; **low-involvement purchases** (gum, a soda) are often habitual or impulsive, with little research. Marketing to each looks different: high-involvement buyers want detailed information and comparison content; low-involvement buyers respond more to availability, packaging, and simple repetition.

Buying behavior is also shaped by cultural, social (reference groups, family), personal (age, lifestyle), and psychological (motivation, perception, beliefs) factors. A reference group's influence explains why a teenager's sneaker choice tracks their friend group more than any ad campaign.

example.problem: A company sells both budget notebooks (low-involvement) and high-end laptops (high-involvement). Design a different marketing approach for each.
steps: For notebooks: emphasize availability, price, and simple, repeated brand exposure since buyers won't research extensively.
For laptops: provide detailed spec comparisons, reviews, and financing options since buyers will research heavily and want to reduce risk of a wrong high-stakes purchase.
example.answer: Market notebooks through price, availability, and repetition; market laptops through detailed comparisons, reviews, and reassurance, matching effort to each purchase's involvement level.

keyTerms.def: The five stages consumers move through: need recognition, search, evaluation, purchase, post-purchase evaluation.
A purchase with high cost or risk that triggers extensive search and evaluation.
Post-purchase doubt about whether a decision, especially an expensive one, was correct.

practice.q: A car buyer researching for weeks before deciding is exhibiting behavior typical of:
choices: Need recognition without a decision process
practice.explain: High-cost, high-risk purchases like cars trigger extensive search and evaluation, the hallmark of high involvement.

practice.q: Marketing to low-involvement purchases should emphasize:
choices: Availability, price, and repeated brand exposure
practice.explain: Low-involvement buyers do little research, so simple, repeated, available cues matter more than detailed comparisons.

practice.q: A warranty reassuring a buyer after a big purchase primarily addresses:
practice.explain: Warranties reduce post-purchase doubt, which is exactly what cognitive dissonance describes.

lessons.title: Market Segmentation and Targeting
lessons.intro: Trying to sell one product to everyone usually means it appeals strongly to no one. Segmentation splits a market into groups worth treating differently.

sections.heading: Bases for Segmentation
body: **Market segmentation** divides a broad market into groups with similar needs, using four common bases: geographic (region, climate), demographic (age, income, family size), psychographic (lifestyle, values, personality), and behavioral (usage rate, brand loyalty, purchase occasion). Most real segmentation combines several bases rather than relying on one.

A useful segment must be measurable, substantial enough to be worth targeting, accessible through some marketing channel, and differentiable in its response to marketing. A segment that can't actually be reached with a distinct message isn't useful no matter how clearly defined it is.

sections.heading: Targeting Strategies
body: After segmenting, a firm chooses a targeting strategy: **undifferentiated** (one offer for the whole market), **differentiated** (separate offers for several segments), **concentrated/niche** (one offer for one segment), or **micromarketing** (tailored to individuals or very local markets). The choice depends on company resources, product variability, and competitive intensity.

A small firm often does best with concentrated targeting, focusing all resources on serving one segment excellently rather than spreading thin across many, while a larger firm with more resources can afford differentiated targeting across several segments simultaneously.

example.problem: A small startup makes vegan protein bars and has limited marketing budget. Choose and justify a targeting strategy versus a major snack conglomerate that sells many bar types.
steps: The startup has limited resources, which favors concentrating on one well-defined segment rather than spreading across many.
Target health-conscious vegans specifically (a niche, differentiable segment reachable through vegan/fitness-focused channels) rather than trying to appeal broadly.
The conglomerate, with more resources, can afford differentiated targeting across multiple segments (athletes, dieters, kids) with separate product lines.
example.answer: The startup should use concentrated/niche targeting on health-conscious vegans; the larger conglomerate can afford differentiated targeting across multiple segments.

keyTerms.def: Dividing a broad market into groups sharing similar needs, using geographic, demographic, psychographic, or behavioral bases.
Focusing marketing resources on serving a single, well-defined market segment.
Developing separate marketing offers for several distinct market segments.

practice.q: Segmenting a market by age, income, and family size uses which basis?
practice.explain: Age, income, and family size are demographic variables.

practice.q: A small firm with limited resources typically benefits most from:
practice.explain: Limited resources favor focusing intensely on one well-matched segment rather than spreading thin.

practice.q: For a segment to be useful, it must be measurable, substantial, accessible, and:
choices: Differentiable in its response to marketing
Composed of at least one million people
Identical to a competitor's target segment
practice.explain: A segment must respond differently to marketing than other segments to justify targeting it separately.

lessons.title: Positioning and Marketing Research
lessons.intro: Once you know who you're targeting, you need a clear claim on a specific spot in their mind — and real data, not guesswork, to know if that claim is landing.

sections.heading: Positioning and the Positioning Statement
body: **Positioning** is the distinct place a brand occupies in the target customer's mind relative to competitors, often built around a clear point of difference (fastest, cheapest, most durable, most sustainable). A **positioning statement** typically follows the form: for [target segment], [brand] is the [category] that [point of difference], because [reason to believe].

Positioning fails when it tries to claim everything at once — 'cheap and premium and fastest' collapses into no clear position at all. A **perceptual map**, plotting brands on two key attributes customers care about, helps a firm see open, undefended positions relative to competitors.

sections.heading: Marketing Research Basics
body: **Marketing research** systematically gathers data to test assumptions before committing budget: **primary research** (surveys, interviews, experiments run specifically for this question) and **secondary research** (existing data like census figures or industry reports, cheaper but not tailored to the exact question).

Good research design matters: a biased sample (surveying only existing loyal customers about a new competitor threat) will systematically miss the perspective that matters most. Research should precede major positioning or segmentation decisions, not just follow them to justify a decision already made.

example.problem: Write a positioning statement for a meal-kit company targeting busy young professionals, differentiated by 15-minute prep time.
steps: Identify the target: busy young professionals with limited cooking time.
Identify the point of difference: 15-minute prep versus the 30-45 minutes typical competitors require.
Assemble the statement using the standard form with a reason to believe (pre-chopped ingredients and simplified recipes).
example.answer: For busy young professionals, [Brand] is the meal-kit service that gets dinner on the table in 15 minutes, because every ingredient arrives pre-chopped and every recipe is simplified to five steps or fewer.

keyTerms.def: The distinct place a brand occupies in the target customer's mind relative to competitors.
A visual plot of brands against two key attributes, revealing open or crowded competitive positions.
Data gathered specifically to answer a current research question, such as a survey or experiment.

practice.q: A positioning statement that tries to claim 'cheapest and most premium' typically:
choices: Collapses into no clear position at all
Is the recommended approach for all brands
practice.explain: Contradictory claims dilute rather than sharpen a brand's position in customers' minds.

practice.q: Existing census data used to study a new market is an example of:
practice.explain: Secondary research uses existing data gathered for another purpose, unlike primary research collected specifically for the current question.

practice.q: Surveying only existing loyal customers about a competitive threat risks:
choices: A biased sample that misses the perspective that matters most
Eliminating the need for a perceptual map
practice.explain: Loyal customers aren't representative of the broader market whose perspective on a new threat actually matters.

units.title: Product and Price
units.summary: Two of the four Ps decide what you're actually selling and what you charge for it. Learn how products evolve over their life cycle and how to set a price with real numbers, not guesswork.

lessons.title: Product Life Cycle and New Product Development
lessons.intro: Every successful product eventually gets copied, commoditized, or replaced — and the marketing strategy that launched it is not the strategy that should defend it years later.

sections.heading: The Product Life Cycle
body: The **product life cycle** describes four stages after launch: **introduction** (slow sales, heavy promotion spending, often a loss), **growth** (rapid sales increase, competitors enter), **maturity** (sales peak and flatten, competition is intense, price competition increases), and **decline** (sales fall as new alternatives replace the product).

Strategy should shift by stage: introduction favors building awareness and trial; growth favors building brand preference and expanding distribution; maturity favors defending share through differentiation or cost efficiency; decline favors harvesting profit or exiting. Applying an introduction-stage strategy (heavy trial promotion) to a mature product wastes money the product no longer needs to spend.

sections.heading: New Product Development
body: New products typically move through idea generation, screening, concept testing, business analysis, product development, test marketing, and commercialization. Skipping test marketing to save time is a common cause of expensive launch failures, since it's the stage that catches problems (wrong price, weak positioning) while the cost of failure is still small.

**Diffusion of innovation** describes how different customer groups adopt at different speeds: innovators and early adopters take a risk on something new, while the early and late majority wait for proof, and laggards adopt last, if ever. Marketing a genuinely new product to the mass market too early, before it has traction with early adopters, is a common launch mistake.

example.problem: A once-popular soda brand is in the maturity stage, with flat sales and heavy competition, and management wants to keep spending like it's still in the introduction stage.
steps: Recognize the stage mismatch: introduction-stage strategies (heavy trial-generation spending) don't fit a mature product with existing high awareness.
Recommend a maturity-appropriate strategy instead: differentiate through a line extension or improve production efficiency to compete on cost, rather than continuing heavy awareness spending.
example.answer: Shift from introduction-style trial spending to a maturity-stage strategy — differentiation or cost efficiency — since the product's awareness is already established and the real fight is holding share.

keyTerms.def: The four stages a product passes through: introduction, growth, maturity, and decline.
Launching a product in a limited market to catch problems before a full-scale rollout.
The pattern by which different customer groups (innovators, early adopters, majority, laggards) adopt a new product at different speeds.

practice.q: A product with flat sales and intense price competition is most likely in which stage?
practice.explain: Flat sales and intense competition, especially on price, are hallmarks of the maturity stage.

practice.q: Skipping test marketing to save time risks:
choices: Missing problems (price, positioning) while they're still cheap to fix
Eliminating the need for a marketing plan
Improving the product life cycle automatically
practice.explain: Test marketing exists to catch costly mistakes early; skipping it means those mistakes surface after a full launch, when they're expensive to fix.

practice.q: Early adopters, as opposed to the late majority, are customers who:
choices: Take a risk trying something new before it has widespread proof
Only buy after the product is thoroughly established
practice.explain: Early adopters are willing to try new products before broad market proof exists, unlike the late majority, who wait.

lessons.title: Branding and Product Strategy
lessons.intro: A brand is more than a logo — it's the bundle of associations that lets a customer trust a product before they've even tried it, and that trust is worth real money.

sections.heading: Brand Equity
body: **Brand equity** is the added value a brand name gives a product beyond its physical attributes — the reason customers will pay more for a branded aspirin than an identical generic one. High brand equity comes from brand awareness, perceived quality, strong brand associations, and loyalty built up over repeated positive experience.

Firms protect brand equity through consistent quality and consistent messaging over time; a single quality failure or a jarring rebrand can erode equity built over years, because trust accumulates slowly and can be lost quickly.

sections.heading: Line and Brand Extension
body: A **line extension** introduces a new item in an existing product category under an existing brand (a new flavor of an established chip brand); a **brand extension** uses an established brand name to enter a different product category (a shoe brand launching an athletic apparel line). Both leverage existing equity but risk diluting it if the new item doesn't fit the brand's core association.

A luxury watch brand launching a budget product line risks confusing customers about what the brand actually stands for, weakening the premium association that justified the original higher price — a cautionary case for keeping extensions consistent with brand meaning.

example.problem: An athletic shoe brand known for performance and durability is considering launching a budget line sold in discount stores to grow volume. Assess the risk using brand equity concepts.
steps: The brand's equity rests on a premium, performance-durability association.
A budget discount-store line contradicts that association and risks diluting the perceived quality that supports the premium price on the core line.
example.answer: The budget line risks eroding brand equity by contradicting the premium performance association; if pursued, it should use a distinct sub-brand to protect the core brand's meaning.

keyTerms.def: The added value a brand name gives a product beyond its physical attributes.
A new item in an existing product category launched under an existing brand name.
Using an established brand name to enter a different product category.

practice.q: Brand equity is best defined as:
choices: The added value a brand name provides beyond the product's physical attributes
The total revenue a brand earns in a year
The number of SKUs a brand sells
practice.explain: Brand equity is the extra value customers attach to the name itself, not a revenue or share figure.

practice.q: A shoe brand launching an athletic apparel line under its own name is an example of:
practice.explain: Entering a new product category under an existing brand name is a brand extension, distinct from a line extension within the same category.

practice.q: A key risk of brand or line extension is:
choices: Diluting brand equity if the new item doesn't fit core associations
Eliminating the need for quality control
Automatic price increases across the whole brand
practice.explain: Extensions that contradict what a brand stands for can weaken the very equity they're meant to leverage.

lessons.title: Pricing Strategies and Tactics
lessons.intro: Price is the only one of the four Ps that generates revenue directly instead of costing money, and getting it wrong by even a few percentage points can wipe out a product's profit.

sections.heading: Cost-Plus Pricing and Markup
body: **Cost-plus pricing** sets price by adding a target markup to unit cost. If a retailer's unit cost is $40 and it wants a 50% markup on cost, price = cost × (1 + markup) = $40 × 1.50 = $60. Markup can also be expressed on selling price instead of cost, which gives a different number for the same margin, so it's important to know which base is being used.

Cost-plus pricing is simple and guarantees a margin per unit, but it ignores what customers are actually willing to pay and what competitors charge — a firm can price itself out of the market with a mathematically correct but strategically blind cost-plus number.

example.problem: A boutique's unit cost for a jacket is $80. It wants a 60% markup on cost. What is the selling price?
steps: Apply the formula: price = cost × (1 + markup rate).

sections.heading: Break-Even Analysis and Skimming vs. Penetration
body: **Break-even volume** is the number of units that must be sold to cover total fixed costs, given the contribution margin (price minus variable cost) per unit: break-even units = fixed costs ÷ (price − variable cost). If fixed costs are $50,000, price is $25, and variable cost per unit is $15, contribution margin is $10, so break-even = $50,000 ÷ $10 = 5,000 units.

For new products, firms choose between **price skimming** (start high to capture customers with high willingness to pay, then lower price over time — common for new tech) and **penetration pricing** (start low to build volume and market share fast, then potentially raise price — common when competitors can enter easily and market share matters more than early margin).

example.problem: A new gadget has fixed costs of $200,000, sells for $80, and costs $50 per unit to produce. How many units must be sold to break even, and would skimming or penetration pricing better fit a market with strong early tech enthusiasts and slow-to-follow competitors?
steps: Contribution margin = price − variable cost = $80 − $50 = $30 per unit.
Break-even units = fixed costs ÷ contribution margin = $200,000 ÷ $30 ≈ 6,667 units.
Since competitors are slow to follow and tech enthusiasts will pay a premium early, price skimming fits better than penetration pricing.
example.answer: About 6,667 units to break even; price skimming is the better fit given slow competitor entry and early adopters willing to pay a premium.

keyTerms.def: Setting price by adding a target markup percentage to unit cost.
Units needed to sell so total contribution margin covers fixed costs: fixed costs ÷ (price − variable cost).
Launching at a high price to capture high-willingness-to-pay customers before lowering it over time.
Launching at a low price to build volume and market share quickly.

practice.q: A product costs $50 to make and is priced with a 40% markup on cost. What is the selling price?
practice.explain: Price = cost × (1 + markup) = $50 × 1.40 = $70.

practice.q: Fixed costs are $60,000, price is $20, variable cost per unit is $12. What is the break-even volume?
practice.explain: Contribution margin = $20 − $12 = $8. Break-even = $60,000 ÷ $8 = 7,500 units.

practice.q: Penetration pricing is most appropriate when:
choices: Competitors can enter easily and market share matters more than early margin
The firm faces no competition at all
Customers have very high willingness to pay early on
The firm wants to maximize short-term profit per unit
practice.explain: Penetration pricing builds share fast to establish position before easy competitor entry, trading early margin for volume.

units.title: Place and Promotion
units.summary: A great product at the right price still fails if customers can't find it or never hear about it. Learn distribution channel choices and how to build an integrated communications plan, including digital channels.

lessons.title: Distribution Channels and Supply Chain
lessons.intro: Very few products travel straight from factory to customer. Understanding the layers in between — and who should own them — is the essence of the Place decision.

sections.heading: Channel Length and Intermediaries
body: A **direct channel** sells straight from producer to consumer (a farm's own roadside stand); an **indirect channel** uses one or more intermediaries — wholesalers, distributors, retailers. Intermediaries add cost but also add value: breaking bulk into smaller quantities, providing local availability, and offering credit or expertise that would be expensive for the producer to replicate everywhere itself.

The number of intermediary layers is the channel's length. Longer channels can reach more markets efficiently but reduce the producer's control over price and presentation at the point of sale — a tradeoff between reach and control that firms must actively manage, not ignore.

sections.heading: Distribution Intensity
body: **Intensive distribution** puts a product in as many outlets as possible (gum, soda — convenience matters most). **Selective distribution** uses a limited number of qualified outlets (mid-range appliances, sold through a curated set of dealers). **Exclusive distribution** restricts sales to one or few outlets per market area (luxury cars, certain designer goods), protecting brand image and allowing tighter service standards.

Choosing the wrong intensity undermines positioning: putting a luxury watch in every drugstore would destroy the exclusivity that justifies its price, while restricting a convenience snack to only one store per city would tank its sales by making it hard to find.

example.problem: A premium skincare brand wants to preserve its luxury image while a competitor sells a similar mass-market product everywhere. Recommend a distribution intensity and channel structure.
steps: Given the luxury positioning, intensive distribution would undercut the brand's exclusivity.
Recommend selective or exclusive distribution: a curated set of department stores and the brand's own boutiques, controlling presentation and service standards.
example.answer: Use selective or exclusive distribution through curated department stores and owned boutiques to protect the premium image the intensive-distribution competitor can't match.

keyTerms.def: A distribution path selling straight from producer to consumer with no intermediaries.
Placing a product in as many outlets as possible to maximize convenience and availability.
Restricting sales to one or a few outlets per market area to protect brand image and service quality.

practice.q: A luxury brand best protects its premium image with:
choices: A fully direct-only channel in every case
practice.explain: Limiting outlets protects exclusivity and presentation, which intensive distribution would undermine.

practice.q: Intermediaries add value by:
choices: Breaking bulk, providing local availability, and offering credit or expertise
Always lowering the final price to consumers
Eliminating the need for any producer involvement
practice.explain: Intermediaries perform functions like breaking bulk and providing local reach that would be costly for a producer to do alone everywhere.

practice.q: Longer distribution channels generally trade reach for:
choices: Reduced producer control over price and presentation
practice.explain: More intermediary layers extend reach but reduce how much control the producer keeps over the customer experience.

lessons.title: Integrated Marketing Communications
lessons.intro: A customer who sees a mismatched message on TV, in-store, and on social media loses trust fast. Integrated marketing communications keeps every channel telling the same story.

sections.heading: The Promotion Mix
body: The **promotion mix** includes advertising (paid, non-personal mass communication), personal selling (direct, one-on-one persuasion), sales promotion (short-term incentives like coupons or discounts), public relations (managing reputation through earned, non-paid media), and direct/digital marketing (targeted messages to individuals). Each tool has different strengths: advertising builds broad awareness efficiently, personal selling handles complex, high-value sales, and sales promotion drives short-term action.

**Integrated marketing communications (IMC)** coordinates all these tools so the customer receives one consistent message and experience across channels, rather than a disjointed set of messages that make the brand feel confused or untrustworthy.

sections.heading: Push vs. Pull Strategy
body: A **push strategy** promotes the product to channel intermediaries (retailers, distributors) who then push it to consumers, using trade discounts and cooperative advertising. A **pull strategy** promotes directly to end consumers, building demand that pulls the product through the channel as consumers actively request it from retailers.

Most large campaigns use both: manufacturer advertising creates pull demand from consumers while trade promotions push retailers to stock and feature the product prominently, since pull alone doesn't guarantee shelf space and push alone doesn't guarantee anyone wants to buy it.

example.problem: A new snack brand has strong consumer-facing social media buzz (pull) but retailers aren't stocking it because shelf space is competitive. Recommend a fix.
steps: Recognize the gap: pull demand exists but push effort toward retailers is missing.
Add push tactics: offer retailers a trade discount or slotting incentive and co-op advertising support to secure shelf placement.
example.answer: Add push-strategy tactics like trade discounts to retailers, complementing the existing consumer pull demand so retailers are motivated to stock the product.

keyTerms.def: Advertising, personal selling, sales promotion, public relations, and direct/digital marketing combined to reach customers.
Coordinating all promotional tools so customers receive one consistent brand message across channels.
Promoting a product to channel intermediaries so they push it to consumers, often via trade incentives.
Promoting directly to consumers to build demand that pulls the product through the channel.

practice.q: A trade discount offered to retailers to stock a product is an example of:
practice.explain: Push strategies target intermediaries directly with incentives to stock and promote the product.

practice.q: The main goal of integrated marketing communications is to:
choices: Deliver one consistent message across all promotional channels
Use only advertising and no other promotion tools
Maximize the number of separate, unrelated messages
Eliminate the need for public relations
practice.explain: IMC coordinates tools so the customer experiences a unified message, not disjointed ones.

practice.q: Personal selling is best suited for:
choices: Complex, high-value sales requiring one-on-one persuasion
practice.explain: Personal selling's strength is handling complex, high-stakes purchases directly, unlike mass-reach tools like advertising.

lessons.title: Digital Marketing and Social Media
lessons.intro: Digital channels let a small brand reach a precise audience for a fraction of traditional media cost, but they also demand new metrics and constant testing that TV advertising never required.

sections.heading: Digital Channels and Targeting
body: Digital marketing includes search engine marketing (paid ads and organic SEO), social media marketing, email marketing, content marketing, and display advertising. Its core advantage over traditional mass media is precise targeting — reaching a defined audience segment by interest, behavior, or demographic — and real-time measurement of what's actually working.

**Search engine optimization (SEO)** earns free organic traffic by ranking well in search results, while **pay-per-click (PPC)** advertising buys guaranteed placement and charges only when a user clicks. SEO takes longer to build but has no per-click cost; PPC delivers instant visibility but stops the moment the budget does.

sections.heading: Measuring Digital Performance
body: Key digital metrics include **click-through rate** (clicks ÷ impressions), **conversion rate** (conversions ÷ clicks or visits), and **customer acquisition cost (CAC)** (total marketing spend ÷ number of new customers acquired). These let marketers compare channels on hard numbers instead of impressions of 'engagement.'

A campaign with a high click-through rate but a low conversion rate usually signals a mismatch between the ad's promise and the landing page's actual offer — the ad is attracting clicks, but something after the click (price, message, page design) is failing to close the sale.

example.problem: A social ad gets 10,000 impressions, 500 clicks, and 20 conversions (sales). Calculate the click-through rate and conversion rate, and interpret the result if industry-typical conversion rate for this ad type is 8%.
steps: Click-through rate = clicks ÷ impressions = 500 ÷ 10,000 = 5%.
Conversion rate = conversions ÷ clicks = 20 ÷ 500 = 4%.
Compare to the 8% industry benchmark: 4% is well below typical, suggesting the click-through rate is fine but the landing page or offer is underperforming after the click.
example.answer: Click-through rate is 5% and conversion rate is 4%, which is below the 8% benchmark — the ad attracts clicks fine, but the post-click experience needs improvement.

keyTerms.def: Earning free, organic traffic by ranking well in search engine results.
The percentage of impressions that result in a click: clicks ÷ impressions.
The percentage of clicks or visits that result in a desired action, such as a sale: conversions ÷ clicks.
Total marketing spend divided by the number of new customers acquired.

practice.q: An ad gets 20,000 impressions and 800 clicks. What is its click-through rate?
practice.explain: Click-through rate = clicks ÷ impressions = 800 ÷ 20,000 = 0.04 = 4%.

practice.q: A high click-through rate combined with a low conversion rate usually signals:
choices: A mismatch between the ad's promise and the landing page or offer
That the ad should be paused immediately with no diagnosis needed
That SEO is more effective than PPC in this case
That customer acquisition cost is irrelevant
practice.explain: Clicks show the ad is compelling; low conversion means something after the click is failing to close the sale.

practice.q: SEO differs from PPC advertising in that SEO:
choices: Earns free organic traffic but takes longer to build
Charges per click for guaranteed placement
Provides instant visibility with no ongoing effort
Cannot be measured with any metrics
practice.explain: SEO builds organic rankings over time with no per-click cost, unlike PPC, which buys immediate but paid placement.
